analysis.one_liner: Bans lead, mercury, cadmium, and hexavalent chromium from packaging with phase-in limits and exemptions.
analysis.headline: The bill to phase toxic heavy metals out of packaging had 54 cosponsors from both parties, but it never left the Energy and Commerce Committee and no vote was ever held before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned intentionally adding four toxic heavy metals—lead, cadmium, mercury, and hexavalent chromium—to any package or packaging component, including inks, dyes, coatings, and adhesives. Concentration limits would have tightened in steps over four years, from 600 down to 100 parts per million. Companies could get two-year exemptions where a metal was needed for safety or federal requirements, and packaging made with recycled materials was protected from the limits. Manufacturers would have had to certify compliance to distributors, and the certificates would have been available to the public and the EPA.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who lives near a trash incinerator or landfill, and the public generally. The bill's findings state that heavy metals in packaging end up in incinerator emissions and ash, and in landfill leachate, and that these four metals are known to harm human health. Reducing them at the source would have lowered the toxicity of the waste stream. People who buy packaged goods would also have gained a right to see manufacturers' certificates of compliance.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits intentional addition of lead, cadmium, mercury, or hexavalent chromium to packaging starting two years after enactment, with total concentration capped at 600 ppm, then 250 ppm after three years, then 100 ppm after four years.

The bill's findings state these metals end up in incinerator emissions, ash, and landfill leachate, and are known to cause harmful effects on human health and the environment, so removing them reduces the toxicity of the waste stream.
Requires manufacturers and suppliers to sign certificates of compliance and provide them to distributors, the EPA on request, and members of the public within 60 days of a written request.
Authorizes civil penalties up to $25,000 per violation, with each continuing day counting as a separate violation, and lets the EPA seek court orders to force compliance.
Exempts packaging whose metals exceed the limits only because recycled post-consumer material was added, so the rules would not have discouraged recycling.

analysis.who_pays: Packaging manufacturers and suppliers, who would have had to reformulate packages, inks, coatings, and adhesives to remove the metals within two to four years, and file and maintain certificates of compliance. Companies seeking an exemption would have had to petition the EPA. Any added costs could be passed partly to consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: Reformulation and certification are real costs: packaging makers would have had to redesign products and inks within two years and keep signed compliance certificates on file, with fines up to $25,000 per violation per day for failures.

Some packages may genuinely need a listed metal for safety or function; the bill allows two-year EPA exemptions for those cases, renewable only after six years, which supporters would acknowledge is a judgment call left to regulators.

The bill adds a federal certification and paperwork requirement on top of state rules, though it explicitly does not stop states from setting stricter standards, so companies could face multiple overlapping requirements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are ordinary transition costs: reformulating packaging over a phased two-to-four-year schedule, with escape valves for safety-critical uses and recycled content. The benefit is removing four metals the bill describes as known health hazards from the waste stream before they reach incinerator ash and landfill leachate. On its face the design is balanced, and the phased timeline gives industry room to adapt. The bill's serious flaw is not its content but that it never got any committee action at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to two of its subcommittees in October 1991, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Howard Wolpe introduced the bill on October 3, 1991, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On October 18, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness and the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials.
The bill drew 54 cosponsors, including 11 Republicans, 42 Democrats, and 1 Independent, but the record shows no further action of any kind after the subcommittee referrals.
The Congress ended on January 3, 1993, so the bill died in committee without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Packaging manufacturers and suppliers came out ahead: they avoided the reformulation, certification, and penalty exposure the bill would have imposed. The public did not get the reduction in toxic metals in packaging waste the bill promised.

for.name: Rep. Howard Wolpe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Solid Waste Metals Reduction Act on October 3, 1991, with three original co-introducers.

for.name: 11 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support from the start.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral on October 3, 1991; it was sent to two subcommittees on October 18 and the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that never reported the bill or scheduled any action on it during the 102nd Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start, with 42 Democrats, 11 Republicans, and 1 Independent cosponsoring, but no vote was ever held, so opposition by party cannot be measured; the bill died in committee without a recorded fight.

industries.note: The bill would have banned adding four toxic metals to packages and packaging components, forcing reformulation within two to four years, and required signed certificates of compliance with fines up to $25,000 per violation per day. The industry's avoided cost was the public's forgone health protection, though exemptions existed for cases where a metal is essential for safety.

industries.industry: Heavy-metal ink, dye, pigment, coating, and adhesive makers
industries.note: Inks, dyes, pigments, coatings, adhesives, and stabilizers are expressly covered as packaging components, so suppliers of metal-based colorants and coatings would have had to reformulate or lose packaging customers.

The bill's findings state that heavy metals in packaging show up in incinerator emissions and ash and in landfill leachate; removing them at the source would have reduced the toxicity these facilities handle and the hazards they pose to nearby communities.
Packaging that exceeds the metal limits only because post-consumer recycled material was added is exempt, so the bill protects companies using recycled inputs and keeps the recycling loop open.
